code.title: Nearby drivers with a grid-cell index
code.python:
import math
# Grid-cell index: cell -> drivers, driver -> cell (O(1) move, query scans 9 cells)
CELL = 0.01  # degrees, about 1.1 km
def cell(lat, lon):
    return (math.floor(lat / CELL), math.floor(lon / CELL))

cells = {}      # cell -> set of driver ids
where = {}      # driver id -> (cell, lat, lon)

def update(d, lat, lon):
    c = cell(lat, lon)
    old = where.get(d)
    if old and old[0] != c:
        cells[old[0]].discard(d)       # remove from old cell
    cells.setdefault(c, set()).add(d)  # add to new cell
    where[d] = (c, lat, lon)

def nearby(lat, lon, n):
    cx, cy = cell(lat, lon)
    found = []
    for dx in (-1, 0, 1):              # the cell plus its 8 neighbours
        for dy in (-1, 0, 1):
            for d in cells.get((cx + dx, cy + dy), ()):
                _, a, b = where[d]
                found.append((math.hypot(a - lat, b - lon) * 111, d))
    return sorted(found)[:n]

update("D1", 12.9700, 77.5900)
update("D2", 12.9755, 77.5950)
update("D3", 12.9900, 77.6100)   # far
update("D2", 12.9710, 77.5910)   # D2 moves
print("drivers:", {d: v[1:] for d, v in where.items()})
for dist, d in nearby(12.9705, 77.5905, 2):
    print(d, round(dist, 2), "km")

followUps:
Split the hot cell instead of letting one node carry it. Airports, stadiums and stations create a cell with thousands of drivers and requests.

Options: use a finer cell level for that area (adaptive resolution), give the cell its own dedicated shard, and keep a small queue of waiting drivers inside the airport rather than scanning everyone. Example: 3,000 drivers in one 1.2 km cell, each query computing 3,000 distances, is slow; at a level 7 cell (about 150 m) each query scans roughly 100.

Also cap candidates (take the first 200 by recent ping) and cache the answer for a second.

PostGIS is excellent for geography but it is a disk database, and 250K location writes per second is the wrong load for it.

Every update rewrites an indexed row, creating write amplification, vacuum work and replication lag, while the data is worth only a few seconds. An in-memory cell map handles those writes cheaply and loses nothing important when a node restarts, because drivers re-ping within 4 seconds. I would still use PostGIS for slow data: service areas, pickup zones, analytics, and trip history.

Cells that are plain numbers do not care about the poles, but their shape does: longitude lines converge, so a geohash cell near the pole is very narrow, and a neighbour lookup across the 180 degree line must wrap around.

Fix the wrap by computing neighbours with modular arithmetic on longitude (180 + 1 becomes -179). Near the poles use S2 or H3, which tile the sphere without that distortion. Ride-hailing rarely operates there, so a fixed grid with wrapping is enough in practice. Always compute distance with the haversine formula, not the flat distance.

A square has two kinds of neighbours: 4 sharing an edge and 4 touching only at a corner, at different distances (1 versus 1.41). A hexagon has 6 neighbours, all sharing an edge and all the same distance away.

When you average a value such as demand over the neighbouring cells for surge pricing, squares weight the diagonal ones unfairly and produce blocky artefacts. Hexagons give a smooth, isotropic gradient, so a driver moving across a boundary sees no sudden jump. The cost is that hexagons do not nest perfectly inside bigger hexagons.

The boundary problem: two points a few metres apart can sit in different cells, so searching only the rider's own cell misses a driver right across the line.

Solve it by also reading the neighbouring cells (8 for a square grid, 6 for H3), then filtering by true distance. Pick a cell size at least as large as the search radius so that the ring of neighbours is enough. Example: with a 1.2 km cell and a 1 km radius, 9 cells always cover the circle. The cost is 9 lookups per query, which are cheap in memory.

The main downside is waiting: every rider is delayed by the batch window, usually 1 to 3 seconds, to gain a better overall assignment.

Example: riders R1 and R2, drivers D1 (2 min from R1, 3 min from R2) and D2 (3 min from R1, 9 min from R2). Greedy gives R1 to D1 then R2 to D2: 2+9 = 11. Batching gives R1 to D2 and R2 to D1: 3+3 = 6. The gain is real but only when many requests arrive together. Other costs: the assignment solver needs compute (Hungarian is cubic), and a very short window gains little while a long one annoys riders. Tune it per city and time of day.

Because the offer is stored with a 15 second TTL, a crash simply leaves a state that expires by itself, and nothing is stuck forever.

The driver key returns to AVAILABLE when the TTL ends, and the ride stays REQUESTED, so another matcher instance (or the restarted one) picks it up from a durable queue and offers to the next candidate. If the driver accepts during the crash, the accept goes to the trip service, which does its own compare-and-set (REQUESTED to ACCEPTED); a duplicate offer later fails that CAS. So the worst case is a short delay, never two trips for one driver.

code.title: Dijkstra versus A*: nodes expanded

followUps:
A heuristic is admissible if it never overestimates the true remaining cost, and consistent (monotone) if it also obeys the triangle inequality: h(u) is at most cost(u,v) + h(v) for every edge.

Straight-line distance divided by top speed is admissible because no road beats a straight line at top speed. Consistent implies admissible, not the other way round. With a consistent heuristic A* expands each node at most once and the first time it pops the goal the path is optimal; with one that is only admissible a node may need to be re-opened. Overestimating (say, doubling the estimate) is faster but can return a longer route.

Keep the shape of the hierarchy fixed and recompute only the numbers, which is what customisable contraction hierarchies (CCH) do.

The node order is computed once from the road layout (the slow part, hours). Shortcut weights are cheap to recompute: when a traffic feed changes some edges, re-run a bottom-up weight update that touches only affected shortcuts, in milliseconds to seconds. Another approach is to precompute on free-flow speeds and let a small A* on live data refine the ends of the route, or blend with time-of-day speed profiles stored per edge. Regions are updated independently through an overlay graph.

You expect a very high hit rate, above 95 percent and often 99 percent, because tiles are immutable and the same popular places (cities, highways) are requested over and over.

Example: if 1,000,000 tile requests hit the edge and 1 percent miss, only 10,000 go to the origin, which is 100 times less origin load. Zoomed-in rural tiles are the long tail and are fetched rarely, so they lower the average a little. The hit rate is driven by long TTLs (versioned paths allow a year), cache keys with no cookies or per-user query strings, and an origin shield layer that merges misses from many edges into one.

Never change a tile in place: publish the new data under a new version path and move clients over gradually, keeping the old version alive until usage drops.

Steps: build v43 into map/v43/z/x/y, then publish a small manifest (not cached long) that says which version a client should use; new app builds or a percentage-based flag point clients at v43. Old clients keep requesting v42, which still exists. Delete v42 only after its traffic is near zero. If the tile format or style schema changes, put a format version in the manifest too, so an old client never receives data it cannot parse.

code.title: All-or-nothing seat hold with TTL

followUps:
Always take the seats in one agreed order, for example sorted by seat id, and take all of them in one atomic step.

A deadlock needs a cycle: Alice holds A1 and wants A2 while Bob holds A2 and wants A1. If everybody locks A1 before A2, the cycle cannot form. Better still, make the hold all-or-nothing: a single Redis script checks that every requested seat is free and then sets them all, or sets none. In SQL, use one UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (...) AND status='FREE' and check that the row count equals the number of seats. Add a lock timeout as a safety net.

Money is already taken, so you cannot just fail the request. Try to give the seat back to the same customer if it is still free, otherwise refund automatically.

Flow: the payment webhook arrives, we look up the hold, find it expired. In one transaction check whether the seats are still FREE; if so, convert straight to a booking. If someone else has them, mark the order CANCELLED and issue a full refund, with a clear message and perhaps an offer of alternatives. To shrink the window, extend the hold while the customer is on the payment page, and set hold time longer than the payment timeout. Log every case for monitoring.

Make the waiting room extremely cheap and stateless, and put it on the CDN edge so the origin never sees the crowd.

Serve the queue page as a static file; each visitor gets a signed token holding a random position, so no server needs to remember them. Clients poll with jitter (every 10 to 30 seconds, not every second) or use a lightweight long-poll. Admit by publishing one number, the current allowed position, in a cached file: a user may enter when their position is at or below it. Example: 2,000,000 users polling every 20 seconds is 100K requests per second, all cache hits. Pre-scale the edge before the sale.

You cannot stop all bots, but you can make each one expensive and limit what one person can buy.

Layers: require a verified account created before the sale; bind queue tokens to the account and device, so a token cannot be shared; use CAPTCHA or a proof-of-work step at admission, not at every page; cap tickets per account, card and delivery address (for example 4); rate-limit by IP and by behaviour such as impossible click speed. Verified-fan presales or a lottery remove the speed advantage. Make tickets non-transferable or name-bound if the product allows it.

code.title: Idempotency key table replaying a charge
code.python:
import hashlib, json
# Idempotency-key table: key -> (request hash, state, response)
table = {}
charges = []   # the side effect we must not repeat

def handle(key, body):
    h = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(body, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()[:8]
    if key in table:
        rh, state, resp = table[key]
        if rh != h:
            return 422, "key reused with different request"
        if state == "IN_PROGRESS":
            return 409, "still processing"
        return 200, resp + " (replayed)"      # same key, same body: stored answer
    table[key] = (h, "IN_PROGRESS", None)     # unique insert wins the race
    charges.append(body["amount"])            # the real work
    resp = "charged " + str(body["amount"])
    table[key] = (h, "COMPLETED", resp)
    return 200, resp

print(handle("k1", {"amount": 50}))
print(handle("k1", {"amount": 50}))   # client retry
print(handle("k1", {"amount": 99}))   # misuse
print(handle("k2", {"amount": 20}))
print("charges made:", charges)

followUps:
Put the keys in the same database as the business data when you need correctness, and in front of it a fast cache such as Redis for the repeated reads.

The durable insert with a unique constraint must be in the same transaction as the payment, so a crash cannot leave a charge without its key. Redis alone is fast (under a millisecond) but can lose data on failover, which would let a retry through. A good mix: check Redis first for completed keys (cheap replay), and fall back to the database for the authoritative insert. Expire keys after 24 hours or more with a TTL or a nightly delete.

PUT and DELETE are idempotent by their definition, but POST is not, so a payment creation still needs a key.

PUT /orders/42 with the full body gives the same final state however many times you send it. Even so, side effects hanging off it (an email, a charge) are not automatically safe, and a PUT that carries a relative change (such as increment) breaks the rule. So use the HTTP method semantics where they fit, such as a client-chosen id with PUT, and add an idempotency key for POST requests and for anything that triggers an external action.

The outbox pattern makes a state change and its event commit together, by writing the event into a table in the same database transaction.

Steps: inside one transaction update the order row and insert an outbox row (event id, topic, payload). A separate relay process reads unsent outbox rows, publishes them to the broker, and marks them sent. If the relay crashes after publishing but before marking, it publishes again, so consumers must dedupe by event id. This avoids the dual-write problem, where the database commits but the broker publish fails (or the reverse). The relay can poll the table or read the database log via change data capture.

Flink checkpoints guarantee that its own internal state, such as counters, is restored to a consistent snapshot after a failure, which gives exactly-once state updates inside the job.

They do not guarantee that effects outside Flink happen once. After a restore Flink replays input from the checkpointed offsets, so a sink that writes to a database or calls an HTTP service may see the same record twice. You get end-to-end exactly-once only with a transactional sink (two-phase commit to Kafka) or an idempotent sink (upsert by key). Checkpoints also cost latency and storage.

Store money as integers in the smallest unit (cents), never as floating-point numbers, together with a currency code.

Example: 0.1 + 0.2 in binary floating point is 0.30000000000000004, but 10 + 20 cents is exactly 30. For currencies with no minor unit (yen) or three decimals (dinar) keep the exponent per currency. Rounding happens only at defined places such as tax or FX conversion, using a stated rule (round half even, or half up), and the remainder is kept explicitly: splitting 100 cents three ways gives 34, 33, 33, not 33.33 each. Never let the sum of lines drift from the total.

Shard by account id so that one account's lines live together, and keep each transaction's lines on one shard where you can.

Most payments touch two accounts, which may sit on different shards. Then use an ordered sequence of single-shard steps: move money from the customer account into a clearing account on the same shard, then from clearing to the merchant, with each step idempotent and the clearing account balancing the books. This is a saga, not a distributed transaction. Hot accounts (the platform fee account) are split into many sub-accounts and summed on read. Keep an immutable transaction id across steps for audit and reconciliation.

Without provider-side idempotency you must make the unknown outcome visible by looking it up, never by blindly repeating the charge.

First search by your own reference stored in the provider's metadata field (most providers allow a merchant reference): if a charge exists, adopt it. If the provider offers no lookup either, then a duplicate is a real risk, so do not auto-retry; leave the payment PENDING and resolve with the daily settlement report, or flag it for manual review. Another option is to change provider or wrap it with a deterministic request id in the description. Refund a confirmed duplicate immediately.

Long enough to cover the provider's normal retries and webhooks, usually minutes to a few hours, with a hard deadline in a day or less for cards.

Example schedule: re-check after 10 s, 1 min, 5 min, 30 min, 2 h, then daily until the settlement file arrives, which is the final authority. Until then show the user a clear "processing" state. After the deadline, if the provider shows no trace of the payment, mark it failed and release inventory. Alert on payments pending longer than the deadline. The right length depends on the payment method: bank transfers can take days.

code.title: Autocomplete trie with top-K per node

followUps:
Use edit distance on a small candidate set, because trying every query is far too slow.

Approaches: keep a separate index of known words and, for the prefix typed, look up entries within edit distance 1 or 2 (a BK-tree, a Levenshtein automaton on an FST, or a symmetric-delete index). Example: "appel" is distance 2 from "apple" by one swap. Run it only when the exact prefix returns too few results, and rank by popularity with a penalty per edit. Also learn from logs: if many people retype "pizza" after "piza", store that pair as a correction.

Build the new trie on the side, then swap one pointer, so readers never see a half-built structure.

Steps: a batch job builds the new immutable snapshot and writes it to storage; each server loads it into memory next to the live one; once loaded and checked, an atomic reference swap makes new requests use it, and the old one is freed after in-flight requests finish. This is a blue-green swap and costs roughly double memory for a moment. Roll out server by server and keep the old snapshot for a quick rollback.

Do two things: block it at the serving layer right now, and remove it from the data later.

A blocklist is checked at request time on every server (a small set pushed through a config channel in seconds), so the suggestion disappears without waiting for a trie rebuild or CDN expiry. Purge the CDN cache for the affected prefixes at the same time. Then add the term to the build job's filter so the next snapshot excludes it. Example: a defamatory query trending at 10,000 per hour must be gone in under a minute, which only the blocklist plus cache purge achieves.

Measure whether people actually use the suggestions and whether they save typing, both offline and in live experiments.

Offline: replay logged queries and check how often the final query is among the top 5 suggestions after the user typed k characters (hit rate, mean reciprocal rank). Online: A/B test on acceptance rate (clicks on a suggestion), keystrokes saved per query, time to first result, and the share of queries with no results. Watch guardrails too: offensive suggestion rate and latency at the 99th percentile. A better ranking that is slower or unsafe is not better.

code.title: Event-time windows and a watermark
code.python:
# Event-time tumbling 1-minute windows with watermark = max event time - 10s lateness.
LATE = 10
events = [(5, "c1"), (20, "c2"), (65, "c3"), (58, "c4"), (75, "c5"), (3, "c6")]  # (event_time, id), arrival order
counts, emitted, late = {}, set(), []
max_t = 0
for t, cid in events:
    w = t // 60 * 60                      # window start by EVENT time
    max_t = max(max_t, t)
    wm = max_t - LATE                     # watermark: nothing older should arrive
    if w + 60 <= wm and w in emitted:
        late.append(cid)                  # window already closed: side output
        print("t=%d %s LATE (window %d closed)" % (t, cid, w))
        continue
    counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1
    print("t=%d %s -> window %d, watermark %d" % (t, cid, w, wm))
    for ws in sorted(counts):
        if ws + 60 <= wm and ws not in emitted:
            emitted.add(ws)
            print("  EMIT window", ws, "count", counts[ws])
print("late events:", late)

followUps:
An idle partition holds the watermark back, because the watermark is the minimum across all partitions, so windows never close.

Example: partitions P0 and P1; P0 reaches event time 100, P1 sends nothing and stays at 0, so the overall watermark stays at 0 minus lateness, and nothing is emitted. Fix it by marking a partition idle after a timeout (Flink's idleness setting) so it is ignored in the minimum, or by sending periodic heartbeat events. The trade-off: an idle partition that wakes up with old events will produce late data.

A wrong device clock puts events in the wrong window, and a clock far in the future pushes the watermark forward and makes good events look late.

Defences: record the server receive time too and compute the offset (receive time minus client send time) to correct the client time; clamp or reject events whose timestamp is too far in the future or past; and compute the watermark from the trusted time of a robust statistic (for example per-source), not from a single maximum, so one bad phone cannot close everyone's window. Count and report the dropped events.

The watermark can be wrong in both directions: too fast and good data becomes late, too slow and results are delayed or never emitted.

Failure modes: an idle partition stalls it; one clock far in the future jumps it forward; a network outage delivers hours of mobile clicks at once, and all are late; a skewed partition lags behind the rest. Mitigations are idle detection, allowed lateness plus a late-data side output, a batch recompute that fixes the totals, and alerts on the lateness rate. For billing, the nightly batch is the final source, so a watermark mistake costs freshness, not money.

Test it with known data and compare against an independent calculation.

Steps: replay a fixed sample day with seeded duplicates, out-of-order events and late arrivals, and assert exact expected counts (for example 10,000 clicks with 500 duplicates must give 9,500). Run the same data through the batch job and require the totals to match. Add fault injection: kill a worker mid-run and check that results are unchanged after recovery. In production, keep a continuous stream-versus-batch comparison, and alert when the difference passes a tiny threshold such as 0.1 percent.

Take the ride matching system, since a regional outage tests state, consistency and recovery together.

If one region fails, traffic is shifted by DNS or the global load balancer to another region. Driver locations rebuild within seconds, because drivers re-ping every 4 seconds. Trips in progress live in a database replicated across regions; with asynchronous replication a few seconds of the latest writes may be missing, so on failover we reconcile from the apps (the driver app knows its trip state). Matching continues with slightly stale data; payments pause or queue. We accept a short drop in quality, not wrong double assignment.

Build on managed services where the work is common and the service is not your differentiator, and build in-house where your logic or scale is the product.

Managed: object storage and CDN for map tiles, a managed relational database for the ledger and bookings, a managed queue or Kafka, and the payment provider itself. In-house: the matching and dispatch logic, the routing engine, the autocomplete ranking and the fraud rules, because they carry your competitive edge and need custom tuning. The stream aggregation can start on a managed Flink or similar and move in-house only if cost or control demands it.
